column2: The ninth is the jewel-cow, and the tenth is the cow in her own form; for the liquid cows there are pots, and for the others heaps.
Some learned men also wish for a gold-cow here; and some great sages, one of butter and of oil.
This is the procedure and these are the requisites, always accompanied by mantras and invocation, at every parvan.
They should be given according to faith; they grant enjoyment and liberation, give the fruit of many sacrifices, remove all sins and are auspicious.
At the solstice, at the equinox, on a holy Vyatipata, at the beginning of a yuga, at the beginning of a manvantara, and at eclipses and other parvans,
the jaggery-cow and the others should be given by those with devotion and faith, at holy places or at home, and especially on the Ganga bank.
Having thus given a cow by rule to an excellent Brahmin, circumambulated the Brahmin and pleased him with fees,
with a pleased heart he should bow to the officiating priests and dismiss them. Then, well composed, he should worship the Ganga by rule.
Having looked upon the goddess in her divine form bearing eight forms, with a prastha of shali rice and two prasthas of milk
he should have rice-pudding made and offer honey and ghee, each a pala in measure, with a feeling of devotion;
that pudding, cakes, sweets and rounds, and gold and silver of half a guñja in weight,
sandal, aloe, camphor, saffron, guggulu, bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, rocana and white sandal,
blue lotuses and other fragrant flowers: as able, with great devotion he should cast these into the Ganga,
with this mantra, auspicious one, which is declared in the Purana: "Om, salutations again and again to Ganga, to Narayani, to Shivā."
This same procedure, Mohini, is to be followed month by month, in the morning, with composure, on the full moon or the new moon.
The man who for a year with devotion and joy worships as able, eating only haviṣya food, moderate in diet, observing celibacy,
by day or night, with restraint, Mohini — at the year's end to him this Ganga,
wearing a divine body, divine garlands and garments, adorned with divine jewels, stands before him in visible form, granting boons.
Seeing with his own eyes the Ganga thus visible, bearing a divine body, a mortal becomes one whose task is done, auspicious one.
Whatever desires a mortal wishes, he obtains those; but one without desire obtains liberation in that very birth, a Brahmin.
This procedure, beginning with the jaggery-cow, all that you asked, has been told by me: the worship of the Ganga, the year-long vow giving liberation and pleasing the Lord of Shri.
He should worship as able with perfumes, flowers and the like. He should give ten prasthas of sesame to ten Brahmins,
ten prasthas of barley, and the ten products of the cow, as appropriate; fish, tortoises, frogs, crocodiles and other water creatures,
made as able in gold or silver; if not available, made of flour, and having worshipped them with flowers and so on, the knower of mantras should first cast them into the Ganga with the mantra.
On the day of the chariot procession, if he has the means, he should have made an image of the Ganga mounted on a chariot, facing north.
The sight of her moving about is rare in the world for those of sinful deeds. There is a chariot procession of Durga, and likewise it should be done here.
Having thus done it by rule, without stinginess in wealth, he is at once freed from the ten sins to be described.
Taking what is not given, violence not by rule, and intercourse with another's wife: these are remembered as the threefold sin of the body.
Harsh speech, falsehood, slander in every way, and incoherent talk: this is the fourfold sin of speech.
Coveting another's property, thinking ill in the mind, and attachment to what is false: this is remembered as the threefold sin of the mind.
From these tenfold sins, born over ten million births, one is freed; no doubt here, as Brahma's word.
Worshipped with this mantra, she lifts thirty ancestors before and others after from the cycle of rebirth.
Om, salutation to Dashaharā, to Narayani, to Ganga. The mortal who with this mantra on that day, day and night,
chants fifty thousand times obtains the fruit of the ten dharmas, and lifts ten earlier and later generations from the ocean of existence.
Having duly received this hymn to be told, on that day he should chant it before the Ganga and carry on the worship of Vishnu.

Om, salutation to Shivā, to Ganga, giver of good; salutation to you. Salutation to the Vishnu-formed; to you, Ganga, salutations again and again.
naradapuran:167:70	Salutation to the form of all the gods, to the embodiment of medicine; best of physicians of all diseases of all, salutation to you.
naradapuran:167:71	Destroyer of poison born of the unmoving and moving, salutation to you; to the destroyer of the poison of worldly existence, to life, salutations again and again.
naradapuran:167:72	To her who destroys the threefold affliction, to the mistress of life-breaths, salutations again and again; to peace, to the remover of torment, salutation to you of all forms.
naradapuran:167:73	To the maker of complete purification, salutation to the liberator from sin; to the giver of enjoyment and liberation, to Bhogavati, salutations again and again.
naradapuran:167:74	To Mandakini be salutation; to the giver of heaven, salutations again and again; salutation to her whose form is the three worlds, to Tridashā, again and again.
naradapuran:167:75	Salutation to you who abide in purity, to Kshemavati again and again; to her who abides on the seat of the gods, to Tejovati, salutation to you.
naradapuran:167:76	To the gentle one bearing the linga, to Narayani, again and again; salutation to Vishvamitrā, to you Revati, again and again.
naradapuran:167:77	To the great one, salutation always; to the supporter of the world, again and again; salutation to Vishvamukhi, to you Nandini, again and again.
naradapuran:167:78	To Prithvi, to Shivāmṛtā, to Virajā, again and again; to her who is the first of the beyond and the near, to you Tara, again and again.
naradapuran:167:79	Salutation to you abiding in heaven, to the undivided again and again; to the peaceful, to you the foundation, to the giver of boons, again and again.
naradapuran:167:80	To the fierce one, to the one of (obscure epithet), to the reviver, again and again; to her who goes to Brahma, the giver of Brahman, the destroyer of sin, again and again.
naradapuran:167:81	To the destroyer of the distress of the bowing, to the mother of the world, again and again; to the cleanser, the destroyer of difficulty, the skilful, to you again and again.
naradapuran:167:82	To the foe of all calamities, to the auspicious, again and again; O highest and beyond, to you, giver of liberation, always salutation. May Ganga be before me, and Ganga on both my sides.
naradapuran:167:83	May Ganga be all around me; in you, Ganga, may my standing be. At the beginning, end and middle, you are all, auspicious Gangā.
naradapuran:167:84	You alone are the root Prakriti; you are the Lord Narayana. Ganga, you are the Supreme Self and Shiva; to you salutations again and again.
The one who devoutly reads this hymn daily, or hears it with faith, from the faults arising from body and speech
stationed in ten ways, is freed from all. The sick is freed from disease, one in calamity from calamity,
from enemies and bondage and fears is freed; he obtains all desires, and after death merges in Brahman.
In whose house this hymn is kept written and worshipped, there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor fear even from sins.
On that tenth day, standing in Ganga water, chanting this hymn ten times, even one who is poor or incapable
obtains that fruit, worshipping the Ganga with devotion; the fruit proclaimed by the procedure stated before.
As Gauri, so Ganga; therefore the procedure prescribed properly for worship of Gauri also applies in the worship of Ganga.
As Shiva, so Vishnu; as Vishnu, so Uma; as Uma, so Ganga; here there is no difference.
He who declares a difference between Vishnu and Rudra, between Ganga and Gauri, or between Lakshmi and Gauri, is dull-witted.
In the bright fortnight, by day, on the Ganga's land, in the northern course of the sun, the fortunate give up the body with Janardana in the heart.
The men who give up their breath in the Ganga on a day by rule go to Vishnu's world, praised by those abiding in heaven.
He who dies in the Jahnavi, half-immersed in the water, by fasting, does not go to rebirth and attains union with Brahman.
The goal of the yoga-disciplined, sattvic, wise man is the goal of the embodied who give up life in the Ganga.
The man who, having undertaken a fast, dies on the Ganga bank, truly attains the highest world together with his ancestors.
The wise man who wishes to give up life by dying in the Ganga — the many births gone and the deaths in all those places —
and even a great time has gone, still he goes; near or far, two yojanas are alike here.
By death in the Ganga here, no deliberation need be made, whether knowingly, unknowingly or by desire.
A mortal who dies in the Ganga finds heaven and liberation. The man who remembers the Ganga as his breaths are being released,
or touches her, even of sinful nature, goes to the supreme goal.
Those wise ones who, having gone to the Ganga, have cast off the body attain equality with the gods; therefore, giving liberation to all, one should serve the Ganga until the fall of the body.
One who dies in the sky, on earth or in water, even a great sinner, attains the imperishable state honoured by Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
The righteous man, living, self-controlled, approved by the good, who contemplates the Ganga in mind, obtains the highest goal.
Even one dying anywhere, when death is at hand, remembering the Ganga with devotion goes to Shiva's or Vishnu's city.
She who came forth from the very rough matted locks of Shambhu, flooded and carried to heaven the sons of Sagara burned by sin.
For as many bones of a man as remain in the Ganga, for so many thousands of years he is honoured in heaven.
One whose bone is carried and cast into Ganga water by men, from that moment his abode is in heaven.
One of good deeds whose bone reaches Ganga water has no return from the world of Brahma at all.
Whose bone meets Ganga water within ten days (of death) obtains a fruit like that of dying in the Ganga.

Then, having bathed, sprinkled with the five products of the cow, joined with gold, honey, ghee and sesame, placing the bone-pinda in a leaf-cup, looking toward the direction embraced by the ghost-hosts,
saying "Salutation to Dharma," entering the water he should cast it with "May he be pleased with me." Then, bathing, seeing the holy banyan tree Akshaya, he should give a fee.
Having done thus, for one dwelling in the city of ghosts the goal in heaven is like that of Mahendra.
Taking the flow as boundary, up to four cubits: there Narayana is the lord, never another lord.
One should not accept gifts there, even with life-breaths risen to the throat. On the fourteenth of the bright half of Bhadra, as far as the water extends,
so far one should know the womb (garbha), that is called "far"; the bank is up to a hundred and a half cubits of garbha, then beyond.
This is the opinion of some, goddess, approved in Shruti and Smriti: a "field" (kshetra) extends one gavyūti around from the bank.
Leaving the bank one should dwell in the kshetra; residence on the bank is not approved. The boundary of the kshetra is one yojana wide from the two banks.
All sins whatsoever do not cross the Ganga's boundary; seeing it they flee like forest-dwellers seeing a lion.
Where the Ganga is, O fortunate one, and the austerity-forest of Rama and Shambhu: know that as a perfected field, three yojanas all round.
At a tirtha and at holy shrines, one should not accept gifts; in all occasions, a man should refrain from that.
He who accepts gifts at a tirtha and holy shrines, his tirtha is fruitless, as long as that wealth is said to remain.
From selling the Ganga, goddess, there is a selling of Vishnu; when Janardana is sold, the three worlds are sold.
He who bears on his head the (clay) born from the Ganga's bank bears the form of the Sun, solely for the destruction of darkness.
The man who, having spread dust born of the Ganga sand, pleases his own ancestors and offers pinda-balls, takes them to heaven too.
This, fortunate one, is the supreme glory of the Ganga told to you; the man who reads or hears it goes to that highest abode of Vishnu.
This should be chanted always with devotion by the self-controlled and faithful, by those desiring the Vaishnava or the Shaiva goal, by rule, dear one.
